intro: The third movement of the Symphony No. 1 in C minor, Op. 68, marked Un poco allegretto e grazioso, opens with a clarinet tune over pizzicato cellos. When the clarinet’s tune returns, the repeated notes of the middle section continue above it.

sections.label: A · Clarinet melody over pizzicato cellos
sections.mNote: The second phrase inverts the melody of the first.

sections.label: B · Repeated notes in B major
sections.mNote: Wind notes alternate with descending string arpeggios in 6/8.

sections.label: Link · Wind triplets lead into 2/4
sections.mNote: Strings hint at the opening tune in A♭ minor.

sections.label: A′ · Clarinet theme with trio figures
sections.mNote: Flutes and oboes continue the repeated-note triplets.

sections.label: Coda · A♭ major
sections.mNote: Repeated notes and broken chords close in A♭ major.

cues.title: Opening clarinet phrase and inversion
cues.text: A clarinet plays a five-bar phrase above pizzicato cellos. The answering phrase inverts the melody, so that each rise becomes a fall. Bassoon and horn fill in the harmony, and the upper strings enter near the end of the phrase.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 1, III, bars 1–10; Breitkopf & Härtel collected edition, IMSLP 317803. Phrase lengths and inversion: Kelly Dean Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: First performance, Karlsruhe, 4 November 1876
cues.text: Otto Dessoff conducted the première in Karlsruhe on 4 November 1876. Brahms was forty-three. He had already called the symphony “long and not exactly amiable”, and audiences and critics were divided over it.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel, Boston Symphony programme note: première in Karlsruhe under Otto Dessoff, Brahms’s age on finishing, his own verdict and the conflicting reactions. https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor . Brahms-Institut Lübeck work catalogue, Op. 68: https://brahmsinstitut.de/Archiv/web/bihl_digital/jb_werkekatalog/op_068.html

cues.title: F minor section, bars 45–61
cues.text: In F minor, the strings divide a quick four-note pulse between high and low instruments. The clarinet begins an agitated melody, which the flute and oboe then take over.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, III, bars 45–61; divided string pulsation and wind entries described in Hansen’s score guide. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Middle section in B major, 6/8
cues.text: The middle section moves to B major and 6/8. The winds repeat three notes, and the strings follow with falling broken chords. The beat now divides into threes, where the clarinet’s opening theme moved in twos.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, III, bars 71–86; B-major trio in 6/8. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Levi on the middle movements
cues.text: Hermann Levi admired the finale of the First Symphony, but thought the two middle movements out of place in it. Here Brahms gives the orchestra a clarinet tune, plucked strings and a brief dance in B major.
cues.evidence: Levi’s response to the First Symphony is reported by Marc Mandel, Boston Symphony programme note. https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor

cues.title: Return of the clarinet theme
cues.text: The clarinet’s opening melody returns in A♭ major over its plucked cello accompaniment. Above it, flutes and oboes continue the trio’s repeated notes as triplets, so for a few bars material from both sections sounds together.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, III, bars 115–125; clarinet reprise with the trio figure in upper winds. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Piano four-hand arrangement, 1877
cues.text: In October 1877 Simrock published the full score together with Brahms’s arrangement of the whole symphony for piano four hands. In the arrangement two pianists play all four movements, this clarinet tune included, at one keyboard.
cues.evidence: Brahms-Institut Lübeck work catalogue, Op. 68: first printing of the full score (Simrock, plate 7957) and of the arrangement for piano four hands (plate 7959), both October 1877: https://brahmsinstitut.de/Archiv/web/bihl_digital/jb_werkekatalog/op_068.html

cues.title: Coda, bars 154–164
cues.text: The coda is marked Poco a poco più tranquillo (gradually more tranquil). The violins play the trio’s repeated notes softly, and the lower strings follow with falling broken chords. The harmony turns briefly to D♭ and returns to A♭, and the final cadence comes after an exchange between winds and strings.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, III, coda, bars 154–164; Hansen’s score guide. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: E♭ respelled as D♯
transitions.from: A · Clarinet melody over pizzicato cellos
transitions.to: B · Repeated notes in B major
transitions.how: Clarinet, horn and violin descend through an E♭ chord while the cellos play pizzicato upwards. E♭ is respelled as D♯, the third of B major. The metre changes from 2/4 to 6/8, and three repeated wind notes alternate with descending string arpeggios.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, III, bars 62–78; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: Return to 2/4 with wind triplets
transitions.from: B · Repeated notes in B major
transitions.how: In bars 109–114, D♯ is respelled as E♭ and the strings play a fragment of the opening tune in A♭ minor. The score returns to 2/4, and the winds continue the trio’s repeated notes as triplets. A quiet pizzicato descent in the strings prepares the clarinet’s return in A♭ major.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, III, bars 109–114; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: The clarinet returns beneath the trio
transitions.to: A′ · Clarinet theme with trio figures
transitions.how: The cellos return to their plucked opening pulse in A♭ major. Clarinet and horn bring back the first phrase, and above them flutes and oboes continue the trio’s repeated-note triplets. The reprise is shorter than the opening section and omits its F minor episode.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, III, bars 115–153; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: The cadence opens into trio material
transitions.from: A′ · Clarinet theme with trio figures
transitions.how: The approaching cadence opens into the trio’s repeated notes, now in violins, with descending arpeggios below. Brahms marks poco a poco più tranquillo. The strings move briefly towards D♭, and flutes, clarinets and bassoons follow and lead back to A♭.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, III, bars 154–164; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

source.title: Brahms, Symphony No. 1, Simrock first-edition full score, plate 7957 (1877)
source.locator: III. Un poco allegretto e grazioso, pp. 35–42; opening, bars 45, 71, 87, 109, 115 and 154.

timeline.note: Clarinet melody above plucked cellos, with bassoon and horn harmony.
The opening tune passes to the violins while the clarinet adds a counterline in triplets.
The tune turns to F minor above quick repeated notes in divided strings.
In the trio, repeated wind notes alternate with descending string broken chords.
The expanded trio gains trumpet support above active string arpeggios.
Strings anticipate the opening while winds retain the trio’s repeated-note pattern.
The clarinet plays the opening melody again while the flute and oboe keep the triplets from the trio.
In the coda, quiet exchanges between strings and wind return to the trio’s pattern.

composer.epithet: Composer who completed his First Symphony at the age of forty-three and began his Second beside an Austrian lake the following summer.
facts: Piano with Otto Cossel; piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen in Hamburg
Detmold, 1857–59 · Vienna Singakademie, 1863–64 · Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde, 1872–75
Vienna; summers in Baden-Baden, Pörtschach, Mürzzuschlag and Bad Ischl
Four symphonies, four concertos, chamber music, piano pieces, songs and choral works; no opera
composer.background:
In the autumn of 1853 a twenty-year-old pianist from Hamburg arrived at the Schumanns’ home in Düsseldorf with an introduction from Joseph Joachim. Johannes Brahms played his own music to them. Robert Schumann heard in him a composer of the future and announced him that October in an article called Neue Bahnen (New Paths). Publishers became interested. Brahms was now expected to fulfil a public prophecy before most of the public had heard any of his music. His piano sonatas were large-scale works. The symphonies Schumann expected took much longer to arrive.

Brahms was born in Hamburg in 1833. His father, Johann Jakob, earned his living playing instruments including the horn and double bass. His mother, Christiane Nissen, was a seamstress. He studied piano with Otto Cossel and then piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen, who grounded him in Bach, Mozart and Beethoven. He played, arranged and accompanied for money. A tour with the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi in 1853 brought him to Joachim, and Joachim sent him on to Düsseldorf.
